claim: The ratio between κ and λ light chain (LC)-expressing B cells varies considerably between species.
source: The ratio between κ and λ light chain (LC)-expressing B cells varies considerably between species.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge in the abstract without specific citation to experimental data in this manuscript.

claim: Kidins220 was identified as an interaction partner of the BCR.
source: We recently identified Kinase D-interacting substrate of 220 kDa (Kidins220) as an interaction partner of the BCR.
evidence: References prior work by the authors (Fiala et al., 2015).

claim: In vivo ablation of Kidins220 in B cells resulted in a marked reduction of λLC-expressing B cells.
source: In vivo ablation of Kidins220 in B cells resulted in a marked reduction of λLC-expressing B cells.
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1A and referenced prior publication (Fiala et al., 2015).

claim: Kidins220 knockout B cells fail to open and recombine the genes of the Igl locus, even in genetic scenarios where the Igk genes cannot be rearranged.
source: Kidins220 knockout B cells fail to open and recombine the genes of the Igl locus, even in genetic scenarios where the Igk genes cannot be rearranged or where the κLC confers autoreactivity.
evidence: Supported by experimental data in Figures 2 and 3 showing germline transcript levels and κ-KO mouse experiments.

claim: Igk gene recombination and expression in Kidins220-deficient B cells is normal.
source: Igk gene recombination and expression in Kidins220-deficient B cells is normal.
evidence: Supported by data in Figure 1 and Figure 2 showing similar Igk germline transcripts and κLC expression between CTRL and B-KO.

claim: Kidins220 regulates the development of λLC B cells by enhancing the survival of developing B cells.
source: Kidins220 regulates the development of λLC B cells by enhancing the survival of developing B cells and thereby extending the time-window in which the Igl locus opens and the genes are rearranged and transcribed.
evidence: Supported by apoptosis data in Figure 4—figure supplement 1A and BCL2 rescue experiments in Figures 4 and 5.

claim: Kidins220 guarantees optimal pre-BCR and BCR signaling to induce Igl locus opening and gene recombination during B cell development and receptor editing.
source: Further, our data suggest that Kidins220 guarantees optimal pre-BCR and BCR signaling to induce Igl locus opening and gene recombination during B cell development and receptor editing.
evidence: Supported by signaling data in Figure 8 showing reduced ERK phosphorylation and ROS levels, and receptor editing experiments in Figures 6 and 7.

claim: The BCR is composed of two immunoglobulin heavy chains and two Igκ or Igλ light chains.
source: Antigen recognition in B cells is mediated by the B cell antigen receptor (BCR), composed of two immunoglobulin (Ig) heavy chains (HC) and two Igκ or Igλ light chains (LC).
evidence: This is established knowledge about BCR structure.

claim: The BCR forms a complex with the associated Igα and Igβ heterodimer to transmit signals for B cell development, proliferation, survival, and activation.
source: They form the BCR complex together with the associated Igα and Igβ heterodimer to transmit signals for B cell development, proliferation, survival, and activation.
evidence: This is established knowledge about BCR signaling.

claim: Each B cell expresses a BCR with a given specificity acquired by progressive rearrangement of V, D, and J gene segments in the bone marrow.
source: Each B cell expresses a BCR with a given specificity, which is acquired by a progressive rearrangement of the variable (V), joining (J) and, in case of the HC, diversity (D) gene segments of the BCR HC and LC loci in the bone marrow (BM) (reviewed in Clark et al., 2014; Herzog et al., 2009).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations to review articles.

claim: RAG1 and RAG2 proteins are the key enzymes that facilitate V(D)J recombination.
source: The key enzymes that facilitate V(D)J recombination are recombination-activating gene 1 (RAG1) and RAG2 proteins (Oettinger et al., 1990; Schatz et al., 1989).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: V(D)J recombination is initiated at the pro-B cell stage.
source: V(D)J recombination is initiated at the pro-B cell stage (Rolink et al., 1999).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation.

claim: An in-frame rearrangement at the HC genes leads to the expression of a µHC that binds to the λ5 and VpreB components of the surrogate light chain.
source: An in-frame rearrangement at the HC genes leads to the expression of a µHC that is binding to the λ5 and VpreB components of the surrogate light chain (Karasuyama et al., 1990; Reth et al., 1985; Tsubata and Reth, 1990).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: The pre-BCR complex is first expressed on large pre-B cells.
source: Together with the Igα/β signaling subunits, these chains form the pre-BCR complex, which is first expressed on large pre-B cells.
evidence: This is established knowledge about B cell development.

claim: Signals from the pre-BCR and IL-7 receptor induce a proliferative burst followed by cell cycle attenuation, promoting LC V- to J-gene segment rearrangement in the small pre-B cell stage.
source: Signals from the pre-BCR and the interleukin (IL)–7 receptor (IL-7R) induce a proliferative burst that is followed by cell cycle attenuation, promoting LC V- to J-gene segment rearrangement in the small pre-B cell stage (Flemming et al., 2003; Ma et al., 2010; Mandal et al., 2009; Ochiai et al., 2012; Reth et al., 1985; Reth and Nielsen, 2014).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by multiple citations.

claim: A productive rearrangement leads to the pairing of the pre-existing HC with the newly generated LC, forming the IgM-BCR expressed first on immature B cells in the BM.
source: A productive rearrangement leads to the pairing of the pre-existing HC with the newly generated LC, forming the IgM-BCR expressed first on the immature B cells in the BM (reviewed in Herzog et al., 2009; Matthias and Rolink, 2005).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations to review articles.

claim: LC locus opening and recombination during B cell development and receptor editing is dependent on transcription factors including Ikaros, Aiolos, IRF-4, IRF-8 and E2A.
source: LC locus opening and recombination during B cell development and receptor editing (a process changing the specificity of the BCR by secondary LC VJ-gene rearrangements) is dependent on transcription factors including Ikaros, Aiolos, interferon regulatory factor (IRF)–4, IRF-8 and E2A (Bai et al., 2007; Beck et al., 2009; Inlay et al., 2004; Johnson et al., 2008; Lazorchak et al., 2006; Lu et al., 2003; Ma et al., 2006; Ma et al., 2008; Mandal et al., 2009; Pathak et al., 2008; Quong et al., 2004; Stadhouders et al., 2014).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by multiple citations.

claim: Genetic mouse models individually lacking some transcription factors show impaired LC locus opening, affecting λLC expression more severely.
source: Genetic mouse models individually lacking some of these transcription factors show impaired LC locus opening, affecting λLC expression more severely (Beck et al., 2009; Lu et al., 2003; Pathak et al., 2008; Quong et al., 2004).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: The activity of transcription factors regulating LC locus opening is directly or indirectly regulated by pre-BCR and BCR signaling.
source: The activity of these transcription factors is directly or indirectly regulated by pre-BCR and BCR signaling.
evidence: This is inferred from the literature and supported by subsequent citations.

claim: Mice lacking a signaling competent pre-BCR or BCR, or lacking signaling molecules downstream including SLP65, BTK and PLCγ2, are characterized by an altered LC expression.
source: Mice lacking a signaling competent pre-BCR or BCR, or lacking signaling molecules downstream of the pre-BCR or BCR including the adapter protein SLP65, Bruton's tyrosine kinase (BTK) and phospholipase Cγ2 (PLCγ2), are characterized by an altered LC expression (Bai et al., 2007; Dingjan et al., 2001; Hayashi et al., 2004; Kersseboom et al., 2006; Xu et al., 2007).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by multiple citations.

claim: Mice deficient in SLP65 show reduced LC germline transcripts especially from the Igl locus.
source: Specifically, mice deficient in SLP65 show reduced LC germline transcripts especially from the Igl locus (Hayashi et al., 2004; Kersseboom et al., 2006; Stadhouders et al., 2014).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: The absence of BTK severely reduces Igl germline transcripts and LC expression.
source: Likewise, the absence of BTK, a kinase that is recruited by SLP65, severely reduces Igl germline transcripts and LC expression (Dingjan et al., 2001; Kersseboom et al., 2006; Stadhouders et al., 2014).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: The concurrent ablation of both SLP65 and BTK abrogates Igk and Igl germline transcription and BCR surface expression.
source: The concurrent ablation of both SLP65 and BTK abrogates Igk and Igl germline transcription and BCR surface expression (Kersseboom et al., 2006; Stadhouders et al., 2014).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: PLCγ2 is recruited to SLP65, regulating the calcium signaling downstream of the pre-BCR and BCR.
source: PLCγ2 is recruited to SLP65, regulating the calcium signaling downstream of the pre-BCR and BCR (Hashimoto et al., 2000; Xu et al., 2007).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: PLCγ2-knockout mice show a strong reduction of λLC B cells and a mild reduction of Igk germline transcripts.
source: PLCγ2-knockout (KO) mice show a strong reduction of λLC B cells and a mild reduction of Igk germline transcripts (Bai et al., 2007; Xu et al., 2007).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: The combined deficiency of BTK and PLCγ2 almost completely abrogated LC expression.
source: The combined deficiency of BTK and PLCγ2 almost completely abrogated LC expression (Xu et al., 2007).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation.

claim: Pre-BCR signaling is important for the induction of LC VJ-gene rearrangement at both LC loci (Igk and Igl).
source: Pre-BCR signaling is important for the induction of LC VJ-gene rearrangement at both LC loci (Igk and Igl).
evidence: This is inferred from the preceding discussion of signaling molecule knockouts.

claim: The ratio between the usage of the two LCs diverges greatly among species.
source: However, the ratio between the usage of the two LCs diverges greatly among species (Sun et al., 2013) and the regulation of their differential expression is still not fully understood.
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation.

claim: The primary B cell repertoire in mice is dominated by the κLC that is roughly ten to 20 times more frequent than the λLC.
source: The primary B cell repertoire in mice is dominated by the κLC that is roughly ten to 20 times more frequent than the λLC (McGuire and Vitetta, 1981; Sun et al., 2013).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: λLC B cell generation is favored when rearrangement at the Igk locus is unsuccessful, or when the immature κLC-containing BCR confers autoreactivity.
source: It is generally accepted that λLC B cell generation is favored when rearrangement at the Igk locus is unsuccessful, or when the immature κLC-containing BCR confers autoreactivity (Luning Prak et al., 2011; Nemazee, 2006).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: Extending the life-span of B cell precursors by overexpression of BCL2 promotes the generation of λLC B cells.
source: Extending the life-span of B cell precursors by overexpression of the anti-apoptotic protein B cell lymphoma 2 (BCL2), promotes the generation of λLC B cells (Ait-Azzouzene et al., 2005; Derudder et al., 2009; Dingjan et al., 2001).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: Limiting B cell survival by genetically abrogating the NF-κB signaling pathway results in mice with a reduced amount of λLC B cells.
source: In line with this, limiting B cell survival by genetically abrogating the NF-κB signaling pathway, results in mice with a reduced amount of λLC B cells (Derudder et al., 2009).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation.

claim: The generation of λLC B cells mainly depends on the ability and kinetics of the LC locus opening, the life-span of developing B cells, and the efficiency of receptor editing during tolerance induction.
source: Based on these observations, the generation of λLC B cells mainly depends on (i) the ability and kinetics of the LC locus opening, (ii) the life-span of developing B cells, and (iii) the efficiency of receptor editing during tolerance induction (Derudder et al., 2009).
evidence: This is inferred from the literature and supported by citation.

claim: Kidins220 was first described as Kinase D-interacting substrate of 220 kDa in neuronal cells.
source: Kidins220 was first described as Kinase D-interacting substrate of 220 kDa in neuronal cells (Iglesias et al., 2000; Kong et al., 2001).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: As a scaffold protein, Kidins220 is implicated in multiple cellular processes like survival, proliferation and receptor signaling, including the antigen receptors of T and B cells.
source: As a scaffold protein, Kidins220 is implicated in multiple cellular processes like survival, proliferation and receptor signaling, among which are also the antigen receptors of T and B cells (Deswal et al., 2013; Fiala et al., 2015; Neubrand et al., 2012).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: The complete genetic deletion of Kidins220 is embryonically lethal.
source: The complete genetic deletion of Kidins220 is embryonically lethal (Cesca et al., 2012).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation.

claim: Conditional mb1Cre-mediated B cell specific Kidins220 KO mice showed reduced BCR signaling.
source: Conditional mb1Cre-mediated B cell specific Kidins220 KO mice (B-KO) showed reduced BCR signaling, and almost complete loss of λLC B cells in the BM and periphery, with only mild effects on the κLC compartment (Fiala et al., 2015).
evidence: This is established knowledge from prior work supported by citation.

claim: Conditional mb1Cre-mediated B cell specific Kidins220 KO mice showed almost complete loss of λLC B cells in the BM and periphery, with only mild effects on the κLC compartment.
source: Conditional mb1Cre-mediated B cell specific Kidins220 KO mice (B-KO) showed reduced BCR signaling, and almost complete loss of λLC B cells in the BM and periphery, with only mild effects on the κLC compartment (Fiala et al., 2015).
evidence: This is established knowledge from prior work supported by citation and confirmed by data in Figure 1A.

claim: B-cell-specific Kidins220 KO mice show an approximately 75% reduction of B cells carrying a λLC-containing IgM-BCR on the cell surface.
source: Despite almost normal B cell numbers, B-cell-specific Kidins220 KO (B-KO) mice show an approximately 75% reduction of B cells carrying a λLC-containing IgM-BCR on the cell surface (Figure 1A; Fiala et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 1A and prior publication.

claim: 98–99% of HCs in immature B cells from CTRL and B-KO mice were annotated to the IgM isotype.
source: Successful purification of immature B cells was confirmed by the annotation of 98–99% of HCs to the IgM isotype (Figure 1B).
evidence: Supported by sequencing data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: In CTRL mice, 83% of all µHCs were co-expressed with the κLC, and the remaining 17% with various subclasses of the λLC.
source: In the CTRL, 83% of all µHCs were co-expressed with the κLC, and the remaining 17% with various subclasses of the λLC (Figure 1C and D).
evidence: Supported by sequencing data shown in Figure 1C and D.

claim: In B-KO B cells, the µHC was almost exclusively co-expressed with the κLC (98%) and only 2% of all cells contained a λLC.
source: In contrast, in B-KO B cells, the µHC was almost exclusively co-expressed with the κLC (98%) and only 2% of all cells contained a λLC.
evidence: Supported by sequencing data shown in Figure 1C and D.

claim: The absence of λLC BCRs on the surface of B cells in B-KO mice reflects absent production of mRNA of Igl from all λLC subclasses.
source: Thus, the absence of λLC BCRs on the surface of B cells in B-KO mice reflects absent production of mRNA of Igl from all λLC subclasses.
evidence: This is inferred from the sequencing data showing lack of λLC transcripts.

claim: Kidins220 does not influence which V(D)J-gene is used for the µHC of the BCR.
source: We obtained very strong correlations for Igh-V- and J-gene usage (r=0.97 and 0.98, respectively), suggesting that Kidins220 does not influence which V(D)J-gene is used for the µHC of the BCR (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: Supported by correlation analysis of sequencing data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1A.

claim: A good correlation of the Igk-V- and J-gene usage (r=0.96 and r=1, respectively) was observed between CTRL and Kidins220-deficient cells.
source: Likewise, we observed a good correlation of the Igk-V- and J-gene usage (r=0.96 and r=1, respectively) between CTRL and Kidins220-deficient cells (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A), confirming a rather intact κLC repertoire.
evidence: Supported by correlation analysis of sequencing data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1A.

claim: B-KO B cells showed a slightly increased use of Igkj5 (14.2%) when compared to CTRL (10%).
source: Still, B-KO B cells showed a slightly increased use of Igkj5 (14.2%) when compared to CTRL (10%) (Figure 1E).
evidence: Supported by sequencing data shown in Figure 1E.

claim: Use of Igkj5 correlates with increased secondary Igk-V- to J-gene rearrangements.
source: Use of Igkj5 correlates with increased secondary Igk-V- to J-gene rearrangements. It frequently occurs before deletion of part of the Igk locus via a recombining sequence recombination and opening of the Igl locus (Prak et al., 1994; Retter and Nemazee, 1998).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: The murine Igl locus comprises one cassette including Iglv2 and Iglv3 upstream of Iglj2-c2 (λ2), and a second cassette containing Iglv1 upstream of Iglj3-c3 (λ3) and Iglj1-c1 (λ1).
source: The murine Igl locus comprises one cassette including Iglv2 and Iglv3 upstream of Iglj2-c2 (λ2), and a second cassette containing Iglv1 upstream of Iglj3-c3 (λ3) and Iglj1-c1 (λ1) (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B; Gerdes and Wabl, 2002; Sanchez et al., 1996).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations and illustrated in Figure 1—figure supplement 1B.

claim: In mature wild type B cells, the different λLCs are used at a frequency of 62%, 31% and 7% for λ1, λ2 and λ3, respectively.
source: In mature wild type B cells, the different λLCs are used at a frequency of 62%, 31% and 7% for λ1, λ2 and λ3, respectively (Boudinot et al., 1994; Sanchez et al., 1996).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: The pattern of λLC usage (62%, 31% and 7% for λ1, λ2 and λ3) was confirmed by sequencing results for immature B cells in CTRL mice.
source: This pattern was confirmed by our sequencing results for immature B cells in CTRL mice (Figure 1D).
evidence: Supported by sequencing data shown in Figure 1D.

claim: The Igl-V-gene usage showed a preference for Iglv1 over Iglv3 or Iglv2, independent of the presence of Kidins220.
source: The Igl-V-gene usage showed a preference for Iglv1 over Iglv3 or Iglv2, independent of the presence of Kidins220 (Figure 1E).
evidence: Supported by sequencing data shown in Figure 1E.

claim: Kidins220-deficient B cells showed a relative increase of Iglv1-gene usage (88% vs 59% in CTRL).
source: However, Kidins220-deficient B cells showed a relative increase of Iglv1-gene usage (88% vs 59% in CTRL) (Figure 1E).
evidence: Supported by sequencing data shown in Figure 1E.

claim: Both CTRL and B-KO immature B cells preferentially used the Iglj1-gene segment (44% and 69%, respectively).
source: Both CTRL and B-KO immature B cells preferentially used the Iglj1-gene segment (44% and 69%, respectively).
evidence: Supported by sequencing data shown in Figure 1E.

claim: B-KO B cells used Iglj3 more frequently than Iglj2.
source: However, B-KO B cells used Iglj3 more frequently than Iglj2.
evidence: Supported by sequencing data shown in Figure 1E.

claim: In the absence of Kidins220, the genes of the second λLC cassette are favored.
source: These observations suggest that in the absence of Kidins220, the genes of the second λLC cassette are favored (Figure 1E).
evidence: This is inferred from the sequencing data showing increased Iglv1 and Iglj3 usage.

claim: The Pearson correlation coefficient for the Igl-J-gene segments was weak in B-KO cells (r=0.51).
source: Indeed, the Pearson correlation coefficient for the Igl-J-gene segments was weak in B-KO cells (r=0.51) (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: Supported by correlation analysis shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1A.

claim: In the Igl locus, VJ-gene recombination preferentially takes place within the same cassette and is almost absent between cassettes.
source: In the Igl locus, VJ-gene recombination preferentially takes place within the same cassette and is almost absent between cassettes (Reilly et al., 1984; Sanchez et al., 1991).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: Recombination of Iglv1 to either Iglj3 or Iglj1 was almost exclusively detected, whereas Iglv2 and Iglv3 recombined to Iglj2.
source: In line with this, we almost exclusively detected recombination of Iglv1 to either Iglj3 or Iglj1, whereas Iglv2 and Iglv3 recombined to Iglj2 (Figure 1F).
evidence: Supported by sequencing data shown in Figure 1F.

claim: Both CTRL and Kidins220-deficient λLC B cells showed a prominence of Iglv1-Iglj1 joins.
source: Both CTRL and Kidins220-deficient λLC B cells showed a prominence of Iglv1- Iglj1 joins.
evidence: Supported by sequencing data shown in Figure 1F.

claim: Both genotypes showed a clear polyclonal distribution for the κLC, but polyclonality was slightly reduced for the HC and strongly restricted for the λLC in the B-KO immature B cells.
source: Both genotypes showed a clear polyclonal distribution for the κLC, but polyclonality was slightly reduced for the HC and strongly restricted for the λLC in the B-KO immature B cells (Figure 1G).
evidence: Supported by CDR3 frequency analysis shown in Figure 1G.

claim: The repertoire of BCRs bearing a λLC was strongly restricted in the B-KO immature B cells.
source: The analysis of paired HC-LC combinations highlighted that indeed the repertoire of those BCR bearing a λLC was strongly restricted in the B-KO immature B cells (Figure 1H).
evidence: Supported by paired HC-LC CDR3 frequency analysis shown in Figure 1H.

claim: No predispositions for potentially autoreactive BCRs as characterized by longer or more positively charged CDR3s were observed in B-KO mice.
source: We did not observe any predispositions for potentially autoreactive BCRs as characterized by longer or more positively charged CDR3s within their variable domain (Figure 1—figure supplement 1C, D).
evidence: Supported by CDR3 length and charge analysis shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1C, D.

claim: The primary B cell repertoire of B-KO mice showed signs of specific clonal expansion, especially of one single clone containing the Ighv10-1-gene segment.
source: Unexpectedly, the primary B cell repertoire of B-KO mice showed signs of specific clonal expansion, especially of one single clone containing the Ighv10-1-gene segment (Figure 1I).
evidence: Supported by similarity network analysis shown in Figure 1I.

claim: The usage of the Ighv10-1-gene segment has been previously associated with anti-DNA antibodies and herpesvirus infections.
source: The usage of this Igh-V-gene segment has been previously associated with anti-DNA antibodies and herpesvirus infections (Maranhão et al., 2013; Zelazowska et al., 2020).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: Both CTRL and B-KO showed similar frequencies of sequences defined as unproductive rearrangements (92% and 93%, respectively) from the Igh locus.
source: Both, CTRL and B-KO, showed similar frequencies of sequences defined as unproductive rearrangements (92% and 93%, respectively) from the Igh locus.
evidence: Supported by sequencing data shown in Figure 1J.

claim: The frequency of sequences defined as unproductive rearrangements from the Igl and Igk loci was increased in B-KO compared to CTRL cells: 1.2 times for Igk, and 2 times for the Igl locus.
source: In contrast, the frequency of sequences defined as unproductive rearrangements from the Igl and Igk loci was increased in B-KO compared to CTRL cells: 1.2 times for Igk, and 2 times for the Igl locus (Figure 1J).
evidence: Supported by sequencing data shown in Figure 1J.

claim: Unproductive rearrangements within the Igl locus in B-KO cells were caused by a series of premature stop-codons.
source: Deeper investigations revealed that these unproductive rearrangements within the Igl locus were caused by a series of premature stop-codons.
evidence: This is inferred from deeper analysis of the sequencing data.

claim: Genetic ablation of Kidins220 in B cells skews the primary BCR repertoire mainly due to unsuccessful production of λLCs.
source: Taken together, genetic ablation of Kidins220 in B cells skews the primary BCR repertoire mainly due to unsuccessful production of λLCs.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion inferred from all the sequencing data presented.

claim: CTRL and B-KO showed increasing levels of κLC+IgM-BCR+ B cells over time after IL-7 withdrawal in pro-/pre-B cell cultures.
source: CTRL and B-KO showed increasing levels of κLC+IgM-BCR+ B cells over time (Figure 2B).
evidence: Supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: The proportion of λLC+IgM-BCR+ B cells was higher in CTRL compared to B-KO B cells at day 3 of culture after IL-7 withdrawal.
source: The proportion of λLC+IgM-BCR+ B cells was higher in CTRL compared to B-KO B cells at day 3 of culture, suggesting that the in vivo phenotype is B cell intrinsic.
evidence: Supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: Prior to LC VJ-gene rearrangement, the gene locus is opened and germline transcripts are produced.
source: Prior to LC VJ-gene rearrangement, the gene locus is opened and germline transcripts are produced (also known as sterile transcripts that do not encode for any protein but are proposed to possess regulatory functions) (Engel et al., 1999; Schlissel and Baltimore, 1989).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: The relative amount of Igk germline transcript and the kinetics of induction was similar between CTRL and B-KO B cells.
source: The relative amount of Igk germline transcript and the kinetics of induction was similar between CTRL and B-KO B cells.
evidence: Supported by qRT-PCR data shown in Figure 2C and D.

claim: Kidins220-deficient B cells failed to induce germline transcription from the Igl locus to the levels of CTRL cells in pro-/pre-B cell cultures upon IL-7 withdrawal and in sorted pre- and immature B cells.
source: However, Kidins220-deficient B cells failed to induce germline transcription from the Igl locus to the levels of CTRL cells in pro-/pre-B cell cultures upon IL-7 withdrawal and in sorted pre- and immature B cells (Figure 2C and D).
evidence: Supported by qRT-PCR data shown in Figure 2C and D.

claim: The Igk germline transcripts in the CTRL cells peaked at day 2 compared to day 3 for the Igl germline transcripts.
source: The Igk germline transcripts in the CTRL cells peaked at day 2 compared to day 3 for the Igl germline transcripts, in line with the findings that activation of the Igk locus precedes the Igl locus (Engel et al., 2001; Luning Prak et al., 2011; Nemazee, 2006).
evidence: Supported by qRT-PCR data shown in Figure 2C and established knowledge from citations.

claim: LC germline transcription is dependent on the expression of E2A proteins (E12 and E47), which in turn regulate the RAG1 and RAG2 proteins.
source: LC germline transcription is dependent on the expression of E2A proteins (E12 and E47), which in turn regulate the RAG1 and RAG2 proteins that are responsible for VJ-gene recombination (Beck et al., 2009; Hsu et al., 2003; Quong et al., 2004).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: No major differences in the expression of Tcf3 (encodes for E12 and E47), Rag1 and Rag2 mRNA were detected between CTRL and B-KO B cells shortly upon IL-7 withdrawal.
source: We did not detect major differences in the expression of Tcf3 (encodes for E12 and E47), Rag1 and Rag2 mRNA as assayed by qRT-PCR between CTRL and B-KO B cells shortly upon IL-7 withdrawal (Figure 2—figure supplement 1B) nor in directly sorted cells (Figure 2—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: Supported by qRT-PCR data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1B and C.

claim: The proportion of GFP+ cells over the 3 days upon IL-7 withdrawal was comparable between CTRL and B-KO cells in the RAG-activity reporter assay.
source: The proportion of GFP+ cells over the 3 days upon IL-7 withdrawal was comparable between CTRL and B-KO cells. This suggests that RAG protein activity per se is not affected by the absence of Kidins220 (Figure 2—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: Supported by RAG-activity reporter data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1D.

claim: Kidins220 is specifically necessary for Igl locus opening and/or its transcription in developing B cells.
source: Together, these data suggest that Kidins220 is specifically necessary for Igl locus opening and/or its transcription in developing B cells.
evidence: This is inferred from the germline transcript data and RAG activity assay.

claim: The effects of Kidins220 on Igl locus opening are independent of the transcriptional or functional regulation of elements of the recombination machinery.
source: Mechanistically, these effects are independent of the transcriptional or functional regulation of elements of the recombination machinery.
evidence: This is inferred from the data showing normal RAG activity and expression.

claim: The heterozygous ablation of one of the κ alleles did not overall change the already described phenotype of CTRL and B-KO mice.
source: As shown in Figure 3A–H and Figure 3—figure supplement 1B–F, the heterozygous ablation of one of the κ alleles did not overall change the already described phenotype of CTRL and B-KO mice (Fiala et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 3 and Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: B-KO mice showed B cell frequencies and cell numbers comparable to CTRL but a severe reduction of λLC+ B cells.
source: B-KO mice showed B cell frequencies and cell numbers comparable to CTRL but a severe reduction of λLC+ B cells (Figure 3—figure supplement 1B, F; Figure 3A–C,H).
evidence: Supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 3 and Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: κ-KO did not significantly alter the total amount of B220+ B cells in the BM in both CTRL and B-KO mice.
source: In both CTRL and B-KO mice, κ-KO did not significantly alter the total amount of B220+ B cells in the BM (Figure 3B and C).
evidence: Supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 3B and C.

claim: A severe developmental block was observed in the generation of BCR+ B cells in both κ-KO genotypes shown by a decreased proportion of IgM+ (immature and mature) B cells and a corresponding increase in pro-/pre-B cells.

claim: IL-7R expression was higher in pro-B cells and decreased subsequently throughout B cell maturation.

claim: Even though BCL2-transduced B-KO B cells showed a pronounced increase of λLC+ B cells, it was still significantly reduced compared to CTRL cells.
source: However, even though BCL2-transduced B-KO B cells showed a pronounced increase of λLC+ B cells, it was still significantly reduced compared to CTRL cells.
evidence: Supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 4C.

evidence: Supported by qRT-PCR data shown in Figure 4D.

Notably, this effect becomes apparent when the survival defect dependent on Kidins220 is rectified through BCL2 overexpression.

claim: Kidins220 plays a role in the survival of B cell precursors.

source: However, the function of Kidins220 seems to be beyond just facilitating B cell survival, since BCL2 overexpression did not fully rescue λLC expression in Kidins220-deficient primary B cell cultures.
evidence: This is inferred from the incomplete rescue of λLC expression by BCL2.

claim: IgM+IgD+ mature B cells clearly accumulated in the BM of CTRL BCL2-transgenic mice.

evidence: Supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 5D, E and Figure 5—figure supplement 1C, D.

claim: Both the percentages and total cell numbers of both κLC+ and λLC+ B cells were expanded in BCL2-transgenic CTRL mice.

evidence: Supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 5F, G and Figure 5—figure supplement 1E, F, and citations.

claim: In B-KO mice, BCL2-transgenic expression failed to increase the percentage and cell numbers of κLC+ and λLC+ B cells to CTRL levels.
source: In B-KO mice, BCL2-transgenic expression failed to increase the percentage and cell numbers of κLC+ and λLC+ B cells to CTRL levels (Figure 5F and G; Figure 5—figure supplement 1E, F).
evidence: Supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 5F, G and Figure 5—figure supplement 1E, F.

source: While BCL2 overexpression-driven increase in B cell precursors in the BM resulted in increased total number of splenocytes, IgM+, κLC+ and λLC+ B cells as reported in CTRL mice (Ogilvy et al., 1999; Vandenberg et al., 2014; Yabas et al., 2011), this was not the case in the absence of Kidins220 (Figure 5H–M and Figure 5I–P).

claim: The percentage of B cells in the spleen was slightly reduced in both CTRL and B-KO BCL2-transgenic mice because of a concomitant expansion of T cells.
source: The percentage of B cells in the spleen was slightly reduced in both CTRL and B-KO mice because of a concomitant expansion of T cells (Figure 5—figure supplement 1H; data not shown).
evidence: Supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1H.

claim: The amount of transitional B cells was increased in BCL2-overexpressing CTRL mice.
source: The amount of transitional B cells was increased in BCL2-overexpressing CTRL mice (Figure 5N), but their proportion within the B220+ B cells was reduced both in CTRL and in Kidins220-deficient mice compared to non-transgenic mice (Figure 5N; Figure 5—figure supplement 1J).
evidence: Supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 5N and Figure 5—figure supplement 1J.

evidence: This is a summary conclusion inferred from the BCL2-transgenic mouse data.

evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation.

source: By using κ-macroself mice as recipients for BM reconstitutions from either CTRL or B-KO mice, all developing donor B cells expressing a κLC will recognize the ubiquitously expressed κ-transgene as a self-antigen, initiating receptor editing and generating B cells with solely λLC surface expression to maintain immune tolerance (Ait-Azzouzene et al., 2005).

source: In κ-macroself mice reconstituted with HSC from B-KO mice, total λLC+ B cell numbers were elevated compared to B-KO (Figure 6F).

evidence: Supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 6F and Figure 6—figure supplement 1C.

claim: Kidins220 is needed to rearrange the genes of the Igl locus and thus fulfil the repertoire with innocuous BCRs.

source: Prolonged survival by transgenic BCL2 overexpression alone, or in combination with enforced receptor editing, failed to fully rescue λLC-expression.

claim: Kidins220 is important for BCR-mediated downstream signaling of ex vivo stimulated primary splenic B cells.

evidence: Supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 8A.

source: No major differences were found for the phosphorylation of p65 and IκB which are components of the NF-κB signaling pathway (Figure 8C).

evidence: Supported by phospho-flow data shown in Figure 8D.

claim: B cells from B-KO mice showed a significantly reduced level of ROS during almost all BM developmental stages except for large pre-B cells.
source: B cells from B-KO mice showed a significantly reduced level of ROS during almost all BM developmental stages except for large pre-B cells (Figure 8E).

claim: A significant drop of ROS from the large to small pre-B cells was confirmed, as previously reported.
source: We confirmed a significant drop of ROS from the large to small pre-B cells, as previously reported (Stein et al., 2017).

claim: The drop in ROS from large to small pre-B cells was much more pronounced in Kidins220-deficient developing B cells.
source: This drop was much more pronounced in Kidins220-deficient developing B cells.
evidence: Supported by ROS measurement data shown in Figure 8E.

claim: ROS were maintained at very low levels throughout B cell development in the BM of Kidins220-deficient mice.
source: ROS were maintained at very low levels throughout B cell development in the BM of Kidins220-deficient mice.
evidence: Supported by ROS measurement data shown in Figure 8E.

claim: Splenic naïve B cells of Kidins220-sufficient and -deficient mice showed similar low ROS levels.
source: Splenic naïve B cells of Kidins220-sufficient and -deficient mice showed similar low ROS levels.
evidence: Supported by ROS measurement data shown in Figure 8E.

claim: One of the main production sites of intracellular ROS are the mitochondria.
source: One of the main production sites of intracellular ROS are the mitochondria (Bae et al., 2011).

source: Interestingly, previous reports pointed toward a connection between Kidins220 and mitochondrial function in neuronal cells (Duffy et al., 2011; Jaudon et al., 2021).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

source: However, we did not detect differences between CTRL and B-KO mice, suggesting a rather normal mitochondrial function (Figure 8—figure supplement 1).

claim: Kidins220-deficient B cells produce less ROS due to impaired pre-BCR and BCR-mediated signaling.
source: These results might indicate that Kidins220-deficient B cells produce less ROS due to impaired pre-BCR and BCR-mediated signaling.

source: Reduced pre-BCR and BCR signaling might in turn prevent the opening and recombination of the Igλ locus in developing B cells.

claim: BTK overexpression slightly increased the relative amount of κLC+ B cells in both CTRL and B-KO cultures at day 3 after IL-7 withdrawal.

source: In the presence of Kidins220, the proportions of λLC+ cells were stronger increased than those of κLC+ B cells.
evidence: Supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 9.

source: In contrast, BTK overexpression in B-KO cells failed to rescue the amount of λLC B cells to CTRL levels.
evidence: Supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 9.

claim: The findings from BTK overexpression emphasize the double function of Kidins220 in B cell development by regulating (pre-) BCR signaling and by supporting B cell survival.
source: These findings again emphasize the double function of Kidins220 in B cell development by regulating (pre-) BCR signaling and by supporting B cell survival.
evidence: This is inferred from the BTK overexpression data.

claim: Deleting Kidins220 in B cells results in a severe reduction of λLC B cells despite normal generation of κLC B cells, generating a skewed antibody repertoire.
source: We have previously discovered that the transmembrane protein Kidins220 binds to the BCR and regulates BCR signaling (Fiala et al., 2015). Deleting Kidins220 in B cells (B-KO mice) results in a severe reduction of λLC B cells despite normal generation of κLC B cells, generating thus a skewed antibody repertoire.
evidence: This is a summary statement supported by citation and data throughout the manuscript.

claim: The absence of Kidins220 specifically prevents opening and/or transcription of the Igl locus.
source: Our data indicate that the absence of Kidins220 specifically prevents opening and/or transcription of the Igl locus.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion inferred from the germline transcript data.

claim: Single-cell analysis confirmed a clear preference for the recombination of Iglv1-gene in WT mice.
source: Our single-cell analysis of the frequencies of Igl-V-gene recombination has confirmed a clear preference for the recombination of Iglv1-gene in WT mice (Boudinot et al., 1994; Sanchez et al., 1996).
evidence: Supported by sequencing data and citations.

claim: The preference for Iglv1 recombination also holds true for B-KO mice.
source: This also holds true for B-KO mice.
evidence: Supported by sequencing data.

claim: The preference for Iglv1 recombination results from the cooperative function of the λ1-3 and λ2-4 enhancers.
source: The current model proposes that this preference results from the cooperative function of the λ1-3 and λ2-4 enhancers, which surround the Igl-V-gene segments 3' and 5' of the λ1 and λ3 family and are bound by the same transcription factors (Collins and Watson, 2018; Haque et al., 2013).

claim: The distance of the λ2-4 enhancer to the λ1-3 enhancer might preclude that Igl gene recombination 5' of the λ2-4 enhancer profit from transcription factors and co-factors of the recombination machinery bound to the λ1-3 enhancer.
source: The distance of the λ2-4 enhancer to the λ1-3 enhancer might preclude that Igl gene recombination 5' of the λ2-4 enhancer profit from transcription factors and co-factors of the recombination machinery bound to the λ1-3 enhancer.
evidence: This is speculated based on the model of Igl locus organization.

claim: The rearrangement of the Iglv1 to Iglj1c1-gene segment eliminates the intervening sequence comprising the Iglj3c3-gene segment, resulting in the accumulation of λ1 LC B cells.
source: The rearrangement of the Iglv1 to Iglj1c1-gene segment eliminates the intervening sequence comprising the Iglj3c3-gene segment, resulting in the accumulation of λ1 LC B cells.
evidence: This is established knowledge about Igl locus recombination.

claim: A relative increase in the usage of the genes of the λ3-family compared to the λ2-family was observed in B-KO versus CTRL mice.
source: Interestingly, we observed a relative increase in the usage of the genes of the λ3-family compared to the λ2-family in B-KO versus CTRL mice.
evidence: Supported by sequencing data shown in Figure 1.

claim: The recombination of the Igl-V-gene segments that are 5' of the λ2-4 enhancer is more dependent on Kidins220 expression than the others.
source: This observation suggests that the recombination of the Igl-V-gene segments that are 5' of the λ2-4 enhancer is more depended on Kidins220 expression than the others.
evidence: This is inferred from the sequencing data showing differential λ-family usage.

claim: Pre-BCR and BCR signaling are reduced in the absence of Kidins220 making the recombination of λ2-family V-genes unlikely.
source: A possible explanation for this observation is that pre-BCR and BCR signaling are reduced in the absence of Kidins220 making the recombination of λ2-family V-genes unlikely.
evidence: This is speculated based on the signaling data and λ-family usage.

claim: Iglv1 is recombined to Iglj3c3 more often in Kidins220-deficient mice.
source: Instead, Iglv1 is recombined to Iglj3c3 more often in Kidins220-deficient mice.
evidence: Supported by sequencing data shown in Figure 1.

claim: Single-cell sequencing analysis supports that Kidins220 is dispensable for Igk, but essential for efficient Igl locus opening and gene recombination.
source: Together, our single-cell sequencing analysis supports that Kidins220 is dispensable for Igk, but essential for efficient Igl locus opening and gene recombination.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion inferred from all the sequencing data.

claim: Reduced production of λLC B cells has been previously described in mouse models with genetic deletion of signaling molecules downstream of the pre-BCR and BCR like BTK, SLP65, and PLCγ2.
source: Reduced production of λLC B cells has been previously described in studies using mouse models with genetic deletion of signaling molecules downstream of the pre-BCR and BCR like BTK, SLP65, and PLCγ2 (Bai et al., 2007; Dingjan et al., 2001; Hayashi et al., 2004; Kersseboom et al., 2006; Middendorp et al., 2002; Stadhouders et al., 2014; Xu et al., 2007).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: The combined deletion of some signaling components almost completely abolishes both Igl and Igk germline transcription, LC V-gene recombination, and protein expression.
source: In contrast, the combined deletion of some of these signaling components almost completely abolishes both Igl and Igk germline transcription, LC V-gene recombination, and protein expression (Kersseboom et al., 2006; Stadhouders et al., 2014; Xu et al., 2007).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: The generation of λLC B cells is more sensitive to defects in the signals transmitted by the pre-BCR and/or BCR.
source: These data led to the interpretation that the generation of λLC B cells is more sensitive to defects in the signals transmitted by the pre-BCR and/or BCR (Stadhouders et al., 2014).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation.

claim: Kidins220-deficiency has been previously described to dampen signaling by receptors in neurons, glial cells, adipocytes, T and B cells.
source: Kidins220-deficiency has been previously described to dampen signaling by receptors in neurons, glial cells, adipocytes, T and B cells (Arévalo et al., 2004; Deswal et al., 2013; Fiala et al., 2015; Jaudon et al., 2020; Jaudon et al., 2021; López-Menéndez et al., 2009; Zhang et al., 2021).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: BCR stimulation in a Kidins220 knockdown mature B cell line resulted in dampened activation of the RAS-ERK pathway due to an inefficient coupling of the BCR to the downstream Raf kinases B-Raf and Raf-1.
source: Indeed, BCR stimulation in a Kidins220 knockdown mature B cell line resulted in dampened activation of the RAS-ERK pathway due to an inefficient coupling of the BCR to the downstream Raf kinases B-Raf and Raf-1 (Fiala et al., 2015).
evidence: This is established knowledge from prior work supported by citation.

claim: IgM-BCR-mediated stimulation of primary splenocytes from B-KO mice resulted in less phosphorylation of ERK and PLCγ2, as well as reduced calcium influx compared to CTRL cells.
source: Likewise, IgM-BCR-mediated stimulation of primary splenocytes from B-KO mice resulted in less phosphorylation of ERK and PLCγ2, as well as reduced calcium influx compared to CTRL cells; further highlighting the role of Kidins220 in BCR signaling (Fiala et al., 2015).
evidence: This is established knowledge from prior work supported by citation.

claim: CD25 is upregulated upon pre-BCR signaling.
source: CD25 is upregulated upon pre-BCR signaling (Lee et al., 2015; Rolink et al., 1994), and its expression level is reduced in mice with genetic ablations of BTK, SLP65, or PLCγ2 (Kersseboom et al., 2003; Kersseboom et al., 2006; Middendorp et al., 2002; Stadhouders et al., 2014; Xu et al., 2007).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: (Pre-) BCR signaling controls Rag expression via the MAPK/ERK pathway.
source: It has been already described that (pre-) BCR signaling controls Rag expression via the MAPK/ERK pathway (Mandal et al., 2009; Mazari et al., 2007; Shaw et al., 1999).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: In the absence of Kidins220, the coupling of (pre-) BCR with the MAPK/ERK signaling pathway is defective resulting in insufficient upregulation of proteins needed for LC rearrangement (RAG, E47).
source: In the absence of Kidins220, the coupling of (pre-) BCR with the MAPK/ERK signaling pathway is defective resulting in insufficient upregulation of proteins needed for LC rearrangement (RAG, E47).
evidence: This is inferred from the signaling data and expression data.

source: It has been previously shown that interference with RAS-MEK signaling leads to upregulation of the negative regulator of E47, namely ID3, and a downregulation of Tcf3 (E47) transcripts and protein levels thus prohibiting its transcriptional function for LC rearrangement (Mandal et al., 2009).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation.

claim: A similar scenario to RAS-MEK interference is conceivable in the context of Kidins220-deficiency.
source: A similar scenario is conceivable in the context of Kidins220-deficiency.
evidence: This is speculated based on the signaling defects observed.

claim: Rearrangement at the Igl locus demands higher levels of E2A activity.
source: It is worth noting that rearrangement at the Igl locus demands higher levels of E2A activity (Beck et al., 2009).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation.

source: This further reinforces the notion that in the absence of Kidins220, the levels of RAG and E2A proteins are insufficient for rearranging the Igl locus while the Igk is rearranged normally.
evidence: This is inferred from the data on E2A activity requirements and the observed phenotype.

claim: In mature B cells, BCR activation induces ROS production to fully activate NF-κB signaling.
source: In mature B cells, BCR activation induces ROS production to fully activate NF-κB signaling (Feng et al., 2019; Wheeler and Defranco, 2012).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: ROS might exert a similar role downstream of the pre-BCR as they do for the BCR.
source: Considering the parallels between BCR and pre-BCR signaling, ROS might exert a similar role downstream of the pre-BCR.
evidence: This is speculated based on the parallels between BCR and pre-BCR signaling.

source: Indeed, previous reports have demonstrated that λLC B cell development but not κLC editing depends on NF-κB signals in line with our results (Derudder et al., 2009).

claim: ROS and MAPK/ERK pathways are manifold interconnected.
source: In addition, ROS and MAPK/ERK pathways are manifold interconnected (reviewed in Corcoran and Cotter, 2013).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation to a review.

source: ROS directly leads to the oxidization of certain amino acids in ERK leading to its activation and nuclear translocation (Galli et al., 2008).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation.

source: Furthermore, ROS are well-recognized as inactivators of phosphatases of the MAPK pathway (Kamata et al., 2005; Son et al., 2011) but also of phosphatases regulating BCR signaling (Reth, 2002; Singh et al., 2005) in non-hematopoietic cells.
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: Reduced generation of ROS in the absence of Kidins220 might lead to a higher activity of ERK-directed phosphatases, which eventually leads to the observed reduced phosphorylation of ERK in B-KO mice.
source: Thus, reduced generation of ROS in the absence of Kidins220 might lead to a higher activity of ERK-directed phosphatases, which eventually leads to the observed reduced phosphorylation of ERK in B-KO mice.
evidence: This is speculated based on the ROS and ERK phosphorylation data.

claim: The findings support a mechanistic model in which Kidins220 mediates its effects by enhancing pre-BCR and BCR signaling.
source: Taken together, our findings support a mechanistic model in which Kidins220 mediates its effects by enhancing pre-BCR and BCR signaling.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion inferred from all the signaling data.

claim: It cannot be formally ruled out that Kidins220 might possess direct, signaling-dependent or -independent effects on the Igl locus opening.
source: Still, we cannot formally rule out that Kidins220 might possess direct, signaling-dependent or -independent effects on the Igl locus opening.
evidence: This acknowledges the limitation of the study.

claim: Kidins220 contributes to pre-B cell survival, which is necessary for LC gene recombination.
source: Our data suggest that Kidins220 contributes to pre-B cell survival, which is necessary for LC gene recombination.
evidence: This is inferred from the survival and BCL2 rescue data.

claim: A prolonged life-span in pre-B cells, induced by overexpression of anti-apoptotic BCL2, increases the amount of λLC+ B cells.
source: In fact, a prolonged life-span in pre-B cells, induced by overexpression of anti-apoptotic BCL2, increases the amount of λLC+ B cells (Ait-Azzouzene et al., 2005; Derudder et al., 2009; Dingjan et al., 2001).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: BCL2 overexpression rescues the generation of λLC B cells in scenarios in which NF-κB signaling was abolished during B cell development.
source: BCL2 overexpression rescues the generation of λLC B cells in scenarios in which NF-κB signaling was abolished during B cell development (Derudder et al., 2009).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation.

source: A connection between (pre-) BCR signaling and survival is well recognized (Kraus et al., 2004; Meffre and Nussenzweig, 2002; Yasuda et al., 2008).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

source: In particular, pre-BCR signaling might lead to the activation of the NF-κB pathway, that in turn regulates the transcription of Pim2, a pro-survival protein in pre-B cells (Bednarski et al., 2012; Derudder et al., 2009; Siebenlist et al., 2005).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: Pre-BCR-mediated ERK activation might induce phosphorylation of the pro-apoptotic protein BIM and thereby interfere with its inhibitory interaction with BCL2, resulting in enhanced pre-B cell survival similar to reports on IgM-BCR signaling.
source: Pre-BCR-mediated ERK activation might induce phosphorylation of the pro-apoptotic protein BIM and thereby interfere with its inhibitory interaction with BCL2, resulting in enhanced pre-B cell survival similar to reports on IgM-BCR signaling (Clark et al., 2014; Gold, 2008; O'Reilly et al., 2009).
evidence: This is speculated based on established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: Pre-BCR-mediated ERK signaling might induce Bcl2 transcription itself, thereby prolonging B cell survival during B cell development.
source: In addition, pre-BCR-mediated ERK signaling might induce Bcl2 transcription itself, thereby prolonging B cell survival during B cell development (Gold, 2008; Yasuda et al., 2008).
evidence: This is speculated based on established knowledge supported by citations.

source: Thus, the afore-discussed defects in coupling pre-BCR and/or BCR signaling to ERK activation in Kidins220-deficient B cells could lead to BCL2 levels that are insufficient to protect developing B cells from cell death.

claim: Ex vivo cultured B cell precursor from B-KO mice die faster upon IL-7 withdrawal.
source: Indeed, ex vivo cultured B cell precursor from B-KO mice die faster upon IL-7 withdrawal (Fiala et al., 2015), and we also detected increased amounts of apoptotic cells during BM B cell development in these mice.

source: However, overexpression of BCL2 did not fully rescue λLC-deficiency in B-KO mice, suggesting that prolong survival of B cell precursors is required, but not sufficient, to optimally generate λLC B cells in the absence of Kidins220 expression.

source: The κ and λLCs differ in the physicochemical and structural properties of their CDR3 regions, and λLCs are proposed to be more effective in rescuing BCRs that show autoreactivity (Townsend et al., 2016; Wardemann et al., 2004).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: Genetically forcing receptor editing using κ-deleting (κ-macroself) mice increased the production of B cells using the λLC in Kidins220 competent mice.
source: In line with previous studies, we show here that genetically forcing receptor editing using κ-deleting (κ-macroself) mice increased the production of B cells using the λLC in Kidins220 competent mice (Ait-Azzouzene et al., 2005; Beck et al., 2009).

claim: In the absence of Kidins220, strong autoreactive ligands efficiently induce the downregulation of surface κLC-BCRs indicating successful tolerance induction.
source: In the absence of Kidins220, strong autoreactive ligands efficiently induce the downregulation of surface κLC-BCRs indicating successful tolerance induction.
evidence: Supported by data in Figure 6.

claim: The replacement of the autoreactive κLC by an innocuous λLC was severely impaired in the absence of Kidins220.

claim: The data obtained in the κ-macroself mice are in line with the single-cell repertoire analysis showing that no signs of potentially autoreactive BCRs were found in B-KO mice.
source: The data obtained in the κ-macroself mice are in line with our single-cell repertoire analysis showing that we did not find any signs of potentially autoreactive BCRs in B-KO mice.
evidence: This connects the κ-macroself data with the repertoire analysis.

source: Since Kidins220-deficient B cells do not open the Igl locus efficiently, secondary rearrangement at the Igk locus should be increased.

claim: Kidins220 supports pre-B cell survival and promotes pre-BCR and BCR signaling via ROS and ERK to allow Igl locus opening and λLC expression during both homeostatic B cell development and receptor editing.

claim: The heightened sensitivity of the Igl locus, compared to the Igk locus, to reductions in expression and activity of recombination machinery proteins regulated by pre-BCR and BCR signals explains why the absence of Kidins220 specifically impacts Igl gene rearrangement.
source: The heightened sensitivity of the Igl locus, compared to the Igk locus, to reductions in expression and activity of recombination machinery proteins regulated by pre-BCR and BCR signals (Bai et al., 2007; Beck et al., 2009; Johnson et al., 2008; Novak et al., 2010; Pathak et al., 2008; Vela et al., 2008; Verkoczy et al., 2005), explains why the absence of Kidins220 specifically impacts Igl gene rearrangement.

claim: This study adds to our understanding of the underlying mechanism regulating the differential expression of the κ and λLCs in B cells and the generation of a self-tolerant repertoire.
source: This study adds thus to our understanding of the underlying mechanism regulating the differential expression of the κ and λLCs in B cells and the generation of a self-tolerant repertoire.
